question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [European Trading Companies and their trade commodities/regions]
options: English EIC – Pepper and spices from Malabar Coast
Dutch VOC – Spice trade primarily from Maluku (Moluccas) Islands
Portuguese Estado da India – Silk trade centred at Surat as principal commodity
French Compagnie des Indes – Textile trade from Pondicherry and Chandannagar
wrong_fact: The Portuguese Estado da India's principal commercial interest was the spice trade (especially pepper and cinnamon), not silk. Surat was primarily an English/Mughal trade hub. The Portuguese centered their trade on Goa and the Malabar spice routes, not silk from Surat.
explanation: The English EIC traded heavily in Malabar pepper and later Bengal textiles. The Dutch VOC dominated the spice trade from the Moluccas (nutmeg, cloves). The French traded textiles from Pondicherry and indigo/textiles from Chandannagar. The Portuguese Estado da India's foundational commerce was the spice trade via Cape Route — pepper from Malabar, cinnamon from Ceylon — NOT silk centred at Surat.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Commercial privileges and Farmans granted to European companies]
options: Farman of 1717 – Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar granted EIC duty-free trade in Bengal
Golden Farman (1632) – Sultan of Golconda granted Dutch trading privileges on Coromandel Coast
Farman of 1651 – Mughal authorities allowed English factory at Hugli in Bengal
Farman of 1717 – EIC received right to mint coins at Bombay in addition to trade privileges
wrong_fact: The Farman of 1717 did NOT grant EIC the right to mint coins. The Farman granted duty-free trade in Bengal, Hyderabad (Deccan), and Gujarat, and the right to purchase zamindari around Calcutta. Coin minting at Bombay was a separate, older right. This option incorrectly conflates two distinct privileges.
explanation: The Farman of Farrukhsiyar (1717) was a landmark — it gave EIC duty-free trade in Bengal (against an annual payment of Rs. 3,000), freedom to export/import, and rights to purchase zamindari around Calcutta. The Golden Farman of 1632 from Golconda's Sultan gave Dutch freedom of trade on the Coromandel Coast. The 1651 Farman allowed the English factory at Hugli. The 1717 Farman did NOT include coin-minting rights — that is a fabricated detail.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dastak (passes) abuse and inland trade disputes]
options: Dastak – Free passes issued by EIC for duty-free transit of goods in Bengal
Ali Vardi Khan – Nawab of Bengal who restricted EIC's use of Dastak to prevent revenue loss
Siraj-ud-Daulah – Nawab who attacked Calcutta partly over EIC's abuse of Dastak
Mir Qasim – Nawab of Bengal who abolished all internal transit duties to counter EIC's Dastak advantage
wrong_fact: Ali Vardi Khan did NOT restrict EIC's Dastak use — it was Mir Qasim who strongly protested and eventually abolished all internal duties to level the playing field. Ali Vardi Khan was a pragmatic ruler who kept relations with the EIC relatively stable. He died in 1756 before the Dastak issue reached its peak under Mir Qasim (1760–63).
explanation: Dastak were free passes originally granted for EIC's own trade but widely misused by Company servants for personal trading, depriving the Nawab of customs revenue. Siraj-ud-Daulah attacked Calcutta (1756) partly over EIC's fortification and Dastak misuse. Mir Qasim (1760–63) brilliantly countered EIC's Dastak advantage by abolishing all internal duties — making all merchants equal — which ironically led to war. Ali Vardi Khan (died 1756) maintained tense but workable relations and did not formally restrict Dastak.
